glial-cell.def: A cell in the nervous system that supports neurons rather than carrying messages: glial cells hold neurons in place, supply nutrients, make myelin and clean up waste.

dendrite.def: A branching fiber of a neuron that receives messages from other neurons and carries them toward the cell body.

cell-body.def: The part of a neuron (also called the soma) that holds the nucleus and keeps the cell alive; it sums up the messages arriving from the dendrites.

axon.def: The long fiber that carries a neuron's action potential away from the cell body toward the axon terminals.

myelin.def: A fatty layer, made by glial cells, wrapped in segments around many axons. It insulates the axon and makes action potentials travel much faster. Damage to it causes multiple sclerosis.

axon-terminal.def: A knob at the end of a branch of the axon, where vesicles release neurotransmitter into the synapse.

sensory-neuron.def: A neuron that carries messages from the body's sensory receptors toward the spinal cord and brain (also called an afferent neuron).

motor-neuron.def: A neuron that carries commands from the brain and spinal cord out to muscles and glands (also called an efferent neuron).

interneuron.def: A neuron inside the brain or spinal cord that passes messages between other neurons, such as between sensory and motor neurons in a reflex.

reflex-arc.def: The quick pathway of a simple reflex: a sensory neuron carries the message to the spinal cord, an interneuron passes it on, and a motor neuron moves the muscle, before the brain is involved.

resting-potential.def: The charge across a neuron's membrane when it is not firing, about -70 millivolts: the inside is negative compared with the outside.

threshold-neural.def: The level of charge, about -55 millivolts, that a neuron must reach to fire an action potential.

depolarization.def: A rise in the charge inside a neuron toward zero and beyond, as positive ions flow in; reaching threshold triggers an action potential.

action-potential.def: A brief electrical signal that travels down a neuron's axon when the neuron fires: the inside charge jumps from about -70 to about +40 millivolts and back.

all-or-none.def: The rule that a neuron either fires a full action potential or does not fire at all; every action potential is the same size, whatever the stimulus.

refractory-period.def: A brief time just after an action potential when a neuron cannot fire again, so signals travel one way and in separate pulses.

synapse.def: The junction where the axon terminal of one neuron meets another neuron, including the tiny synaptic gap the neurotransmitter crosses.

neurotransmitter.def: A chemical messenger released from an axon terminal into the synapse that binds to receptor sites on the next neuron.

reuptake.def: The return of leftover neurotransmitter from the synapse into the sending neuron, which ends the message.

excitatory.def: A neurotransmitter that makes the receiving neuron more likely to fire, by depolarizing it; glutamate is the main one.

inhibitory.def: A neurotransmitter that makes the receiving neuron less likely to fire; GABA is the main one.

dopamine.def: A neurotransmitter involved in movement, motivation and reward. Loss of dopamine neurons causes the movement problems of Parkinson's disease.

serotonin.def: A neurotransmitter involved in mood, sleep and appetite.

norepinephrine.def: A neurotransmitter that raises alertness and arousal.

glutamate.def: The brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, important in learning; too much can overexcite neurons.

gaba.def: Gamma-aminobutyric acid, the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter: it calms neural activity. Alcohol and some anti-seizure drugs boost its effect.

endorphins.def: Neurotransmitters that act as the body's natural painkillers and can lift mood, for example during hard exercise.

substance-p.def: A neurotransmitter that carries pain signals in the spinal cord and brain.

acetylcholine.def: A neurotransmitter that makes muscles contract and plays a role in learning and attention.

endocrine-system.def: The body's slower chemical communication system: glands that release hormones into the blood.

hormone.def: A chemical messenger made by a gland and carried in the blood to targets elsewhere in the body; slower and longer-lasting than a neurotransmitter.

pituitary.def: A pea-sized gland at the base of the brain that releases hormones controlling growth and directing other endocrine glands.

adrenaline.def: A hormone (also called epinephrine) released by the adrenal glands in an emergency; it speeds the heart and breathing and prepares the body for action.

leptin.def: A hormone released by fat cells that signals the brain that the body has enough stored energy, reducing appetite.

ghrelin.def: A hormone released by an empty stomach that signals hunger.

melatonin.def: A hormone released in darkness that helps time sleep; levels rise in the evening and fall in the morning.

oxytocin.def: A hormone released during childbirth, nursing and close physical contact, linked to bonding between people.

psychoactive-drug.def: A chemical that changes perception, mood or behavior by acting on the nervous system, usually at the synapse.

agonist.def: A drug that mimics a neurotransmitter or increases its effect, for example by binding to and activating its receptors.

antagonist.def: A drug that blocks a neurotransmitter's effect, for example by occupying its receptors without activating them.

reuptake-inhibitor.def: A drug that blocks reuptake, so the neurotransmitter stays in the synapse longer and keeps acting on the receiving neuron.

stimulant.def: A drug that speeds up the nervous system, raising alertness and heart rate; examples are caffeine, nicotine, cocaine and amphetamines.

depressant.def: A drug that slows the nervous system, reducing alertness and reaction speed; alcohol is the most common.

hallucinogen.def: A drug that distorts perception and can cause sensory images without real input; LSD and psilocybin are examples.

opioid.def: A drug, such as morphine, heroin or fentanyl, that mimics endorphins: it relieves pain, slows breathing and is highly addictive.

tolerance.def: The need for a larger dose of a drug to get the same effect after repeated use, as the brain adapts to it.

withdrawal.def: The unpleasant physical and psychological symptoms that follow stopping a drug the body has adapted to.

multiple-sclerosis.def: A disease in which the immune system damages myelin in the brain and spinal cord, slowing or blocking signals and causing weakness, numbness and vision problems.

myasthenia-gravis.def: A disease in which the immune system attacks acetylcholine receptors where nerves meet muscles, so muscles weaken quickly with use.
